title: What happens to a pipeline when one consumer lags (consumer-group lag, partition rebalancing, back-pressure), and how do you keep the pipeline healthy (scaling consumers, monitoring lag, dead-letter queues for poison records)?
shortTitle: Consumer lag, rebalancing, back-pressure, and keeping a pipeline healthy
keyPoints: Consumer lag is the gap between the latest produced offset and the committed offset, representing unprocessed backlog.
Steadily growing lag means the consumer cannot keep up and the pipeline is falling behind.
Partition rebalancing redistributes partitions when a consumer joins, leaves, or dies, causing a brief processing pause.
Back-pressure propagates slowness upstream so the pipeline runs at the speed of its slowest stage instead of crashing.
You scale consumers horizontally up to the partition count, which sets maximum parallelism.
Poison records are retried a bounded number of times, then routed to a dead-letter queue so they never block the partition.
Cooperative incremental rebalancing reduces pause duration compared to the older stop-the-world rebalance.

s1_definition.oneliner: Lag is unprocessed backlog; rebalancing redistributes partitions; back-pressure slows producers; and you stay healthy by scaling consumers, monitoring lag, and dead-lettering poison records.
s1_definition.profdef:
Consumer lag and pipeline health involve several related mechanisms.

- **Consumer lag** – The gap between the log-end offset (newest message) and the committed offset (last processed), meaning unprocessed backlog per partition.
- **Partition rebalancing** – When a consumer joins, leaves, or misses heartbeats, the group coordinator reassigns partitions among surviving consumers.
- **Back-pressure** – A slow downstream stage signals upstream to slow down so buffers do not overflow and the pipeline degrades gracefully.
- **Dead-letter queue** – A separate topic where poison records are routed after bounded retries so one bad message never blocks its partition.

Keeping the pipeline healthy requires scaling consumers up to the partition count, monitoring lag, making processing idempotent, and handling poison records.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture the National Bank of India's transaction counter where slips arrive on a conveyor belt from Kafka. Consumer lag is the growing pile of unprocessed slips when the clerk is too slow. If a clerk goes on break, the remaining clerks reshuffle who handles which tray: that reshuffle is a rebalance, and during it processing briefly pauses. Back-pressure is the slow clerk telling the conveyor "stop feeding me, I am swamped" so slips do not spill on the floor. When one slip is so garbled it keeps jamming the machine, you set it aside in a reject tray (dead-letter queue) so the rest keep flowing.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Producer (bank app)
       │
       ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Kafka Topic: bank-transactions   │
  │  ┌────┐ ┌────┐ ┌────┐ ┌────┐    │
  │  │ P0 │ │ P1 │ │ P2 │ │ P3 │    │
  │  └──┬─┘ └──┬─┘ └──┬─┘ └──┬─┘    │
  └─────┼──────┼──────┼──────┼───────┘
        │      │      │      │
        ▼      ▼      ▼      ▼
  ┌─────────┐ ┌─────────┐
  │Consumer1│ │Consumer2│  (2 consumers, 4 partitions)
  │ P0 + P1 │ │ P2 + P3 │
  └────┬────┘ └────┬────┘
       │           │
       ▼           ▼
  ┌──────────────────────┐
  │  Bank Database        │
  │  (downstream sink)    │
  └──────────────────────┘

  If Consumer2 dies:
  Rebalance → Consumer1 gets P0+P1+P2+P3
  Lag on P2, P3 grows until scaling

  Poison record flow:
  Record fails 3x → DLQ topic → Alert → Investigation
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Consumer lag is the single most important health signal for a streaming pipeline. Each partition has a newest offset, each consumer group commits the offset it has processed, and lag is the difference: the unprocessed backlog. Small stable lag is fine, but steadily growing lag means the consumer cannot keep up, which at the National Bank of India could make fraud alerts arrive minutes late.

Partition rebalancing happens whenever group membership changes, and the coordinator reassigns partitions so each live consumer owns a share. A naive rebalance causes a brief stop-the-world pause that spikes lag and can reprocess in-flight work, which is why idempotent processing matters. Cooperative incremental rebalancing reduces that pause to milliseconds. The hard constraint is that a partition is owned by exactly one consumer, so partition count sets maximum parallelism. Back-pressure propagates slowness upstream so the pipeline degrades gracefully instead of crashing.

To keep the pipeline healthy, scale consumers up to the partition count, monitor lag with alerts, make processing idempotent, and handle poison records with a dead-letter queue and bounded retries. Monitor the DLQ itself, because a rising rate points to upstream data quality problems rather than isolated bad records.

At the National Bank of India, when a malformed transaction with a null amount kept failing, the consumer retried it three times and diverted it to the dead-letter queue, committing past it so the partition kept flowing. We watched lag closely, used cooperative rebalancing, and attached clear ownership to the DLQ because in a bank a poison transaction must be investigated rather than silently dropped.

Remember one sentence: monitor consumer lag as the first health signal, scale consumers up to the partition count, make processing idempotent, and dead-letter poison records so they never block the pipeline.
